A book for reflection

James Legge presents the Book of Changes as a layered work: King Wan's explanations of the whole figures, the Duke of Chou's readings of their lines, and later commentaries gathered in the appendices. Legge's introduction recounts a long history of transmission and attribution; this guide reports that account as Legge gives it, rather than claiming that every historical detail is settled.

Source: Legge, Preface; Legge, Introduction Chapter I; Legge, Introduction Chapter III

A hexagram joins two three-line figures called trigrams. The lower trigram is read first and the upper sits above it. Each line is either yang, an unbroken stroke, or yin, a divided stroke. Number the six positions from the bottom upward: the first line is at the base and the sixth is at the top. A reading therefore has a direction even when the picture is printed vertically.

Source: Legge, Introduction Chapter II

The eight trigrams pair a line pattern with a primary image in Legge's account.

  • 坤K'un — Earth
  • 震Chen — Thunder
  • 坎K'an — Water
  • 兌Tui — Lake
  • 艮Ken — Mountain
  • 離Li — Fire
  • 巽Hsün — Wind
  • 乾Ch'ien — Heaven

Source: Legge, Introduction Chapter II; Legge, Appendix V

This edition offers the text as a mirror for reflection, not a way to know or control what comes next. A hexagram makes no prediction or guarantee, and it is not medical, legal, financial, or other professional advice. The meaning of a reading belongs to you; its images can help you notice a situation, not decide it for you.

Source: Legge, Preface

If you consult the book, hold a question open enough to explore rather than framing it as a demand for yes or no. Stay with one cast instead of repeating the same question to seek a different answer. Legge's account of Youthful Folly makes repeated requests a question of sincerity and attention; this edition uses that passage as a reminder to pause.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 4, judgement; Legge, Introduction Chapter II

Casting by hand

Use three coins. Choose one face as heads and count it as 3; count tails as 2. Toss all three together and add their values. Record one total for each toss, repeating until six values are written from bottom to top. A total of 6 is changing yin; 7 is stable yang; 8 is stable yin; 9 is changing yang. This coin method is a convenient modern procedure, not Legge's classical stalk ritual.

  1. Assign heads 3 and tails 2.
  2. Toss three coins and add the values.
  3. Write the total as line 1, the bottom line; repeat through line 6.

Source: Legge, Introduction Chapter II; Legge, Appendix III · Section I

For the classical stalk procedure, begin with fifty stalks and set one aside. Work with the remaining forty-nine through three rounds. In each round, divide the bundle into two at random, remove one stalk from the right-hand group and hold it with the set-aside stalk, then count each group in fours; keep the remainder from each group with the removed stalks. Recombine what remains before the next round. After the third round, the remaining count is 24, 28, 32, or 36, giving line values 6, 7, 8, or 9. Repeat the three rounds for each of six lines.

  1. Set one of fifty stalks aside; divide the other forty-nine.
  2. Remove one from the right group, then count both groups by fours and retain each remainder.
  3. Recombine the remaining stalks and repeat until three rounds are complete; map the final count to 6–9.

Source: Legge, Appendix III · Section I; Legge, Appendix III · Section II

The coin method gives changing yin and changing yang equal weight. The stalk method is asymmetric: changing yang (9) is three times as common as changing yin (6). In both methods, the two changing values together make one quarter of all lines.

Probability of each line value by method
Method6 — changing yin7 — stable yang8 — stable yin9 — changing yang
Three coins1/83/83/81/8
Yarrow stalks1/165/167/163/16

Source: Legge, Appendix III · Section I; Legge, Introduction Chapter II

Draw yang as one unbroken stroke and yin as two separated strokes. Mark a 6 or 9 with the word “changing”; leave 7 and 8 unmarked. This uses the same value and changing-line distinction as the app. Place each new line above the last so the first cast value remains at the bottom.

Line values are recorded from the bottom upward; 6 and 9 change, while 7 and 8 remain stable.

Source: Legge, Introduction Chapter II

Reading change

A changing line is an old yin (6) or old yang (9). To form the relating hexagram, flip each changing line once: yin becomes yang and yang becomes yin. This edition uses one simple default. Some traditional schools weigh changing lines differently; no single school is presented here as authoritative.

  1. Read the first hexagram's judgement and image.
  2. Read only the line passages whose positions changed.
  3. Read the relating hexagram's judgement and image as a second view of the situation's movement; do not read its line texts.

Source: Legge, Introduction Chapter II; Legge, Appendix II · Section II

When no line changes, the first hexagram is the complete reading. There is no relating figure to calculate. Stay with its judgement and image rather than treating stillness as a missing answer.

Source: Legge, Introduction Chapter II

When all six lines change, flip all six to find the relating hexagram. For Hexagram 1 or 2, also read its special all-lines-changing passage. That passage belongs to the source's extra seventh paragraph and is not a seventh line.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, all-lines-changing; Legge, The Text, Hexagram 2, all-lines-changing

Take values 7, 7, 7, 7, 9, 7 from bottom to top. The initial figure is Hexagram 1, with only line 5 changing. Read Hexagram 1's judgement and image, then its fifth line. Flip that line to yin: the relating figure is Hexagram 14. Read Hexagram 14's judgement and image. Treat the pair as two images to reflect on, not as a forecast.

Worked values, bottom to top: 7, 7, 7, 7, 9, 7. Initial hexagram 1; changing lines 5; relating hexagram 14.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, line 5; Legge, The Text, Hexagram 14, judgement

Take values 7, 9, 8, 8, 6, 7 from bottom to top. The initial figure is Hexagram 41; lines 2 and 5 change. Read its judgement and image and only those two lines. Flip both changing lines to form Hexagram 42, then read its judgement and image. Consider what the second figure adds to the first without treating either as a prediction.

Worked values, bottom to top: 7, 9, 8, 8, 6, 7. Initial hexagram 41; changing lines 2, 5; relating hexagram 42.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 41, line 2; Legge, The Text, Hexagram 41, line 5; Legge, The Text, Hexagram 42, judgement

The first figure gives one account of how a situation stands; the relating figure gives another image after the marked lines have turned. Ask what becomes clearer when you hold both descriptions together. The relationship is a reflective prompt about change, not a statement of what must happen.

Source: Legge, Introduction Chapter II; Legge, Appendix II · Section II

Glossary

favorable conditions

Legge source form: good fortune; success

A positive quality in the text's situation, not a promise that an event will occur.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, judgement

serious difficulty

Legge source form: evil; misfortune

A warning about the quality of a situation, rather than a forecast.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 29, judgement

a reason to reconsider

Legge source form: occasion for repentance

A prompt to review conduct or limits without treating the result as fixed.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, line 6

no added harm

Legge source form: no error; without blame

The text does not attach blame to the described action or position.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, line 4

a major undertaking

Legge source form: cross the great stream

Legge's image for a consequential passage through difficulty.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 5, judgement

an experienced perspective

Legge source form: meet the great man

A neutral rendering of seeking the counsel or presence of a person of standing.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, line 2

steady, principled conduct

Legge source form: firm and correct

A combination of persistence and ethical alignment in the source.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, judgement

The sixty-four hexagrams

乾 Hexagram 1 — Creative Force

Legge reference: Ch'ien — The Creative

Upper trigram: Ch'ien (Heaven); lower trigram: Ch'ien (Heaven).

Judgement

The judgement of Creative Force brings creative force and the need to know its limits into view. It places favorable conditions within the scene, as the source's assessment rather than a promise about what comes next. Notice where the passage allows movement and where it marks a limit. What does that balance reveal about your question?

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, judgement

Image

The repeated image of Heaven suggests motion renewed each day. Legge turns that movement toward ceaseless activity and the work of perfecting character. In Creative Force, consider how effort can stay alive without becoming force that is never allowed to rest.

Source: Legge, Appendix II · Section I, Hexagram 1

Line 1 — yang (unbroken), bottom

At place 1, a yang line pictures a dragon hidden in the deep, before its time for action. This is at the beginning in Creative Force. The source's verdict is rendered as steady attention; it names the scene, not an event to come. Consider what the image makes clear, and how this place relates to the other five.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, line 1

All six lines changing

The added passage pictures dragons setting aside their heads. Legge reads this as a change from force and pride toward humility, with favorable conditions for the whole figure. Read it only when all six lines change, beside Hexagram 2; it is a separate whole-figure reading, not a seventh line.

Source: Legge, The Text, Hexagram 1, all-lines-changing
